original_question: Remove the current smoothness restrictions in KAM-based arguments and prove non-transitivity and non-mixing properties for the three-dimensional Euler equation in full generality.
target_in_paper: Section 11, Problem 31: "Relax the restrictions on the smoothness index k of the C^k spaces (related to application of the KAM) and prove non-transitivity and non-mixing properties of the 3D Euler in full generality."
correct_elements: The draft is very close to the paper’s actual open problem. It correctly identifies that the issue is the KAM-driven smoothness restriction, that the equation is the three-dimensional Euler equation, and that the desired dynamical conclusions are non-transitivity and non-mixing. It also stays at the right scope and does not drift into neighboring problems such as wandering solutions, steady Beltrami fields, or higher-dimensional embedding phenomena.
missing_details: The paper formulates the problem for the incompressible Euler equation viewed as a dynamical system, not just as a PDE in isolation (Section 1, Eq. (1.1); Section 11, p. 23).
The global setting explicitly mentioned just before Problem 31 is a closed Riemannian 3-manifold M (Section 11, p. 23).
The smoothness restriction is specifically on the index k in C^k spaces; the draft says "smoothness restrictions" but does not state that the relevant phase-space topology is C^k (Problem 31, p. 23).
The existing global KAM-based result quoted in the paper is non-mixing in the C^k topology for non-integer k > 4 (Section 11, p. 23).
That global result is stated for any prescribed value of helicity and sufficiently large energy; the draft omits these qualifiers (Section 11, p. 23).

The paper also singles out a local non-mixing result near a "typical" steady solution on S^3, with the current regularity threshold non-integer k > 10; the draft does not mention this local setting (Section 11, p. 23).

The paper’s nearby context explains that the KAM input is used to obtain continuity of conserved functionals associated with invariant tori of fixed isotopy types; this is the reason the regularity threshold appears (Section 11, p. 23).
To be fully stand-alone, the question should specify that the intended dynamical notions are topological transitivity and topological mixing in the C^k topology.

"In full generality" should be understood relative to the paper’s stated 3D settings and current KAM-imposed C^k thresholds, not as a broad invitation to move to unrelated function spaces, manifolds with boundary, or higher dimensions.
There are no ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, or nilpotency parameters relevant to this problem; the missing data are geometric and functional-analytic rather than algebraic.
refined_question: Let M be a closed Riemannian 3-manifold, and consider the incompressible Euler equation on M, ∂_t v + ∇_v v = -∇p with div v = 0, as a dynamical system on divergence-free vector fields endowed with the C^k topology. The paper notes that current KAM-based results give global non-mixing on any such M for non-integer k > 4, for any prescribed helicity and sufficiently large energy, and also a local non-mixing statement near a "typical" steady solution on S^3 for non-integer k > 10. Can one relax or remove these KAM-imposed restrictions on the smoothness index k of the C^k spaces and prove, in these same global and local 3D settings, the corresponding failure of topological transitivity and topological mixing for the Euler flow?
justification: The draft clearly targets Section 11, Problem 31 (p. 23), and is already very close to the paper’s wording. The nearby paragraph immediately before Problem 31 supplies the crucial hidden scope: the known KAM-based results concern the 3D incompressible Euler flow on closed Riemannian 3-manifolds, with global non-mixing in C^k for non-integer k > 4 at fixed helicity and sufficiently large energy, plus a local non-mixing statement near a "typical" steady solution on S^3 in C^k for non-integer k > 10. Section 1 provides the base Euler notation. This paper does not contain a relevant Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3 for this draft; the nearest official formulation is therefore Section 11, Problem 31.
